title: Board-style — Correcting a false statement about amphoteric hydroxides
question: A student writes: “Because Zn(OH)₂ is amphoteric, it dissolves in excess NaOH. Therefore, every hydroxide that dissolves in excess NaOH must also dissolve in excess NH₄OH.” Which correction is valid?

options.text: The first sentence is correct, but the conclusion is false: Pb(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NaOH yet remains insoluble in excess NH₄OH.
Both sentences are correct because the two alkalis have identical effects on all hydroxides.
The first sentence is false because Zn(OH)₂ is not amphoteric.
Both sentences are false because neither zinc nor lead hydroxide dissolves in excess NaOH.

explanation:
Zn(OH)₂ is amphoteric and dissolves in excess NaOH. However, solubility with one reagent does not guarantee solubility with the other. Pb(OH)₂ provides the counterexample: it dissolves in excess NaOH but remains insoluble in excess NH₄OH.

question: A student tests an unknown solution by adding excess NaOH immediately. The mixture appears colourless. The student concludes that no precipitate forms with NaOH. Which correction is scientifically most appropriate?

explanation:

title: Board-style — Recognising conflicting evidence
question: A solution is labelled ZnSO₄. A student records all of the following on separate portions: 1. NaOH produces a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. 2. NH₄OH produces a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. 3. NH₄OH on a fresh portion produces a white precipitate that remains insoluble even in excess. Which conclusion is best justified?

options.text: The records conflict for a pure zinc salt under the specified conditions; repeat the test and check for a sample or recording error.
All three observations are characteristic of Zn²⁺ and need no verification.
Zinc hydroxide changes into lead hydroxide whenever more NH₄OH is added.
The sample must contain Cu²⁺ because copper hydroxide is white.

explanation:
The first two observations match Zn(OH)₂, which dissolves in excess NaOH and NH₄OH. The third matches Pb(OH)₂ behaviour with excess NH₄OH. These conflicting results do not justify identifying a pure zinc sample as lead; the experiment should be repeated using a fresh, clearly labelled portion.

title: Integrated conceptual identification
question: An unknown colourless salt solution gives a white precipitate with NaOH. The precipitate dissolves in excess NaOH. With NH₄OH, the white precipitate dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution. Which conclusion is justified?

The cation is Ca²⁺ because calcium hydroxide dissolves in excess NaOH.
The cation is Cu²⁺ because copper hydroxide is white.

explanation:
Zn(OH)₂ is white and dissolves in excess NaOH and NH₄OH to give colourless solutions. Pb(OH)₂ remains insoluble in excess NH₄OH, Ca(OH)₂ remains insoluble in excess NaOH, and Cu(OH)₂ is pale blue.
